title: Mapping models: tiers, reasoning, and multimodality

opening.headline: We'll show you how to choose the right model for your task by organizing the many named models into five criteria: class, inference strength, limit, input format, and ID.
body: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google each release multiple models, each with a mix of numbers and aliases in their names. It is difficult to know which model is larger and which model is faster just by looking at the name, and even the same model has separate settings such as inference strength.

In this class, models from three companies are placed on the same rubric and compared. After drawing a large map in classes of large, medium, and light, we look at inference strength, which controls the amount of thinking without changing the model, context and output limits that determine whether an operation can be performed, multimodal input support, and an ID and version that pinpoint the model. At the end, we select the appropriate model for the three tasks of customer inquiry classification, image description, and contract review with evidence.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the role of large, medium, and light model grades
Model grades can be classified by task difficulty and required delay time.
You can determine whether the basis for model selection for the same task is appropriate.

screens.title: too many names
screens.lead: First, let's look at the difficulties that arise when model names are scattered. Read the scene below and think about what criteria you would use to organize it.

visual.alt: The model name chips of the three companies are scattered chaotically and then arranged in three rows: large, medium, and light.

paragraphs: OpenAI introduces Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and Luna. Anthropic has released Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5, while Google offers Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite. If you put all the model names together, there are more than ten.

Just by looking at the name, you can't tell which one is the biggest and which one is the fastest. Moreover, the same model also has separate settings such as effort and thinking_level, so the choice does not end with just one name. This is why many people choose ‘the biggest one’ or ‘what they have heard of’.

The question for this class is this. By what criteria can we start to see a model? The answer lies in first establishing some standards that are common to all three companies. The first criterion is a three-line map: large, medium, and light.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Which method will last longer when a new model comes out: memorizing names or setting up a rubric?

screens.outro: Before setting the criteria one by one, let us recall how we selected the models so far.

screens.title: How I Picked My Models
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had so many model names that you had to choose just one?
items.answer: The more names there are, the more likely people are to pick familiar names or the top of the list. That doesn't mean those choices are wrong, but if you can't explain why you chose them, you have no standard for the next time you ask them to do the same task again. In this class, we will set a standard that allows you to say why you chose something.

items.prompt: Have you ever thought that the biggest model is always the best?
items.answer: OpenAI's model selection guide says that Astra can be used as the default when cost and latency are not an issue, but it also advises choosing a model and inference strength to reduce usage or turnaround time. In other words, the largest model is a choice when conditions are right, but is not always the right answer.

items.prompt: What was a moment when you were uncomfortable with a task because it was slow or expensive?
items.answer: Usually, the inconvenience increases when the same task is repeated hundreds of times or the user has to wait in front of the screen. These actions are a sign that speed of response and cost are as important as quality. In the screens that follow, see which lightweight grade is right for this job.

screens.outro: Now that we have summarized our experience, we move on to the first criterion: model series and grade.

screens.title: Model families and classes: three-line map
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare what grades the models from the three companies are divided into and what roles each plays. The final tab organizes common structures.

visual.alt: Model rating map with three company columns and three rows: large, medium, and light.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body:
OpenAI's model selection guide introduces three models. **Astra** is a top-tier intelligence, a model for ambiguous problems, deep analysis, and ambitious outcomes. **GPT-6.1 Sol** is a high-performance, optimized model that is suitable when you need to manage time and costs while performing complex tasks. **Luna** is a smart and efficient model for well-scoped tasks, classification, and frequent automation.

The guide explains that Luna is the most cost-effective model and Astra is the most powerful. These role descriptions, not the number in your name, are the clues to your grade.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body:
Claude's model overview compares four current models. **Fable 5.1** is introduced as suitable for demanding inference and long-term agent tasks, **Opus 5.5** as suitable for long-term agent-type coding and knowledge tasks, **Sonnet 5.5** as the best combination of speed and intelligence, and **Haiku 5.5** as suitable for high-volume and delay-sensitive tasks such as classification, extraction, and routing.

In the comparison table in the document, the response speed is indicated as Fable 5.1 being slow, Opus 5.5 being average, Sonnet 5.5 being fast, and Haiku 5.5 being the fastest. The same document tells you to start with Opus 5.5 if you're not sure.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body:
Google's **Gemini 4 Argon** is introduced as a flagship inference model for complex software engineering, deep math and science problems, and autonomous multi-level agents. **Gemini 3.8 Flash** is the most intelligent Flash model, targeting long-term software tasks and complex workflows while maintaining the speed and cost-effectiveness of Flash.

**Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite** is a lightweight model built for low latency and low cost. Specify in the description the uses for which latency and API cost are most important, such as subagent tasks and document parsing, bulk processing, and simple data extraction.

tabs.label: common structure
tabs.body:
If you place the three companies side by side, you will see the same three-line structure. **Large** is responsible for deep analysis and demanding inference, **Medium** is responsible for balancing performance, time and cost, and **Light** is responsible for large repetitive tasks and low latency.

As levels go up, responses usually become slower and prices go up. Even if you come across a model with an unfamiliar name, you can determine where to place it by looking for expressions such as ‘deep analysis’, ‘balance’, and ‘high volume/low latency’ in the introduction.

screens.outro: Now that we've drawn a big map of grades, let's look at the strength of reasoning, which is the handle used within the same grade.

screens.title: Inference Strength: Controlling the amount of thinking without changing the model
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the inference strength to low, medium, or high. See how speed, cost, and quality change depending on intensity.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the inference strength scale on the left and the speed, cost, and quality direction arrows on the right.
labels: Experiment with the same input and choose the lightest setting that satisfies the criteria.

stops.body:
This is the lightest setting. The model uses less thought and output per request, so responses are faster and less expensive. OpenAI's guidance table pairs Luna and Low and presents them as a combination suitable for detailed modifications, problem solving with a clear scope, and simple data extraction.

We also add Low to Astra and advise it to be used for concise writing and content conversion that preserves facts and nuances. Lowering the intensity doesn't necessarily mean you'll get a bad answer. If the task is simple, a lower intensity may be sufficient to meet the criteria.

It's a balance between speed and quality. According to Claude's documentation, the default value for Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 is medium, and it instructs you to start from this value and increase or decrease it as needed.

OpenAI's guide recommends pairing GPT-6.1 Sol with Medium for complex technical work and coordinated results to be modified and refined, and Astra with Medium for ambitious projects that require broad context and reliable interaction.

This is an advantageous setting for complex problems. It uses more thinking and output, resulting in slower responses and higher costs. The Claude documentation states that the default for Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5 is high.

The OpenAI guide table is recommended for decisions made between refined results and conflicting evidence by adding Extra high to GPT-6.1 Sol, and for deep analysis with strict requirements by adding Extra high to Astra. All three companies describe increasing intensity as a difficult choice.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen size and strength together, we're pushing the limits of how much the model can handle.

screens.title: Context/output limits and multimodal support
screens.lead: Each row in the table shows the model's limits and input format. Read from top to bottom and make sure there are no limitations that don't fit your task.

visual.alt: Screen highlighting the Context, Maximum Output, and Input Format rows in the model comparison table.

data.caption: Model-specific limits and input formats
rows: Default 65,536 tokens, maximum 1,048,576 tokens when using long decode
data.notes: The context window is the limit on the number of tokens that can be handled at one time, and the maximum output is the upper limit on the number of tokens that can be generated at once. Claude outlines that current models all support text and image input, text output, multilingualism, vision, and tooling. If the limits and input format do not match the task, it cannot be used for that task even if the grade is high. For example, if you need to insert an audio file yourself, you'll first need to make sure you're accepting audio in the Input Format line. Grades tell you the depth of your abilities, but limits and input formats tell you whether you can do the work. So, in model selection, we check two things separately.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the boundaries of the capabilities, we organize the ID and version that pinpoint the model and the overall rubric.

screens.title: Compare model ID and version using the same standard
screens.lead: If you select and expand each item, the criteria used to compare the three companies will be explained one by one. Expand all items to see the entire rubric.

visual.alt: Side-by-side illustration of a list of model ID examples on the left and a common rubric on the right.

items.title: role
items.body: This is the purpose of the model, which you read about in the introduction. We will organize whether it falls into deep analysis, balance, or high volume/low latency. This role, not the number in your name, is what determines your rank.

items.title: speed and price
items.body: The Claude overview provides a table with speeds (slow, medium, fast, fastest) and input/output prices per million tokens. For example, Fable 5.1 has $10 input and $50 output, and Sonnet 5.5 has $2 input and $10 output. Putting speed and price together in the same rubric shows what you get and what you pay as you move up the ranks.

items.title: Inference settings
items.body: The name used is different for each model. Claude uses effort, Gemini uses low, medium, and high levels of thinking, and OpenAI uses low, medium, and extra high. Even though the names are different, they are all knobs that control the amount of thoughts, so write them side by side on the same line and compare them.

items.title: Limits and input format
items.body: Write down the context window, maximum output, and type of input it can receive. This item determines whether the job is possible, so first determine the length and file format the job requires and then filter it out on this line.

items.title: Model ID and version
items.body:
In the API, models are indicated by ID strings, such as `gemini-4-argon` and `claude-opus-5-5`. Claude's documentation provides a separate 'Model IDs and versioning' document that explains the difference between aliases and snapshots. Even if the name of the series is the same, the behavior may change if the version changes, so in tasks that require reproducing the results, record the ID and version.

For example, the Claude Sonnet 5.5 document sets out the changes from the previous Sonnet 5. Examples include forcing tool usage to return errors, and thinking blocks being tied to models and dialogs. This means that the same code may behave differently when the version changes.

screens.outro: Now that the rubric is complete, we explain the basis for selection by applying it to the three tasks.

screens.title: Case commentary 1: Customer inquiry classification and image description
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of selecting a model for both tasks. Select the arrows to cycle through difficulty, delay, and input format.

steps.title: two tasks
steps.body: The first task is to classify thousands of customer inquiries per day into categories such as ‘delivery’, ‘refund’, and ‘technical inquiry’. The second task is to look at the product photos and write a description in one or two sentences. Both tasks are judged by the same items on the rubric.

steps.title: Difficulty and delay in triaging customer inquiries
steps.body: Classification is a single judgment that is simple, repetitive, and large in quantity. So the delay and cost per incident adds up and makes a big difference. No deep analysis is required, so the benefit of large classes is small.

steps.title: Selection of customer inquiry categories
steps.body: The Claude Model Overview introduces Haiku 5.5 for high-volume, delay-sensitive tasks like classification, extraction, and routing. The OpenAI guidance table also pairs Luna and Low for simple data extraction. So we start at a lightweight grade and only move up when the quality isn't up to standard.

steps.title: Input format for image description
steps.body: Image descriptions should check the input format before the difficulty level. This is because a model that cannot receive images cannot be used, no matter how large it is. Claude current models and Gemini 4 Argon support image input. Check this first in the input format row of the rubric.

steps.title: Choice of image description
steps.body: Among the models that passed the input format conditions, we now select difficulty and delay. A one- or two-sentence explanation is not difficult, so a light or medium-sized model that accepts images is suitable. If you have a lot of photos, lean towards lightweight.

steps.title: Write your evidence in three lines
steps.body: The basis for selection is written in three lines: ‘difficulty, delay, and input format.’ For example, 'difficulty is low because it is simple classification, delay and cost are important due to the large number of cases, and the only input is text. Therefore, it is written as 'lightweight grade'. Having your rationale written down like this makes it easy to reevaluate your choices when conditions change.

screens.outro: Now that we've solved the two easy tasks, we move on to reviewing the contract, which is more difficult to judge.

screens.title: Case Commentary 2: Contract Review and Evaluation of Selection Basis
screens.lead: Alternate between two states and compare the good and weak evidence attached to the same choice. The instructor explains a contract review case as an example.

states.label: good basis
states.body:
The case involves finding and organizing risk clauses in dozens of pages of contracts. Good evidence is written like this. 'The input is long, so the context limit must be sufficient, and missing a clause can cause significant damage, so accuracy is more important than cost. Therefore, start from a higher level or higher inference strength.'

The Claude selection paper introduces an approach where accuracy is a priority, so implement from the strongest starting point and then gradually work your way down to an efficient model. OpenAI Guidelines also pairs GPT-6.1 Sol or Astra with high intensity for the task of making decisions between conflicting evidence.

This rationale specifies at least two factors: task difficulty, input length, and cost, which directly lead to selection. So others can read it and check its validity.

states.label: weak evidence
states.body:
If you use it this way for the same task, it is a weak basis. 'It is safe because it is the largest model.' Or, 'It's best because it has the latest version number in the name.' Or, 'I'm copying because another team is already using it.'

These sentences only talk about the model's size, name, or someone else's choice, and are not connected to the needs of this task. What's missing is how many pages the contract is, how long you can wait, and what the cost of an error is.

OpenAI guidance recommends that you first consider how often the task will occur, how quickly you need results, how you will use the results, and how important quality is to you. Good evidence is the answer to this question, weak evidence is the answer that skips this question. Additionally, any basis goes through a process of being confirmed by experimenting with the same input.

screens.outro: Now that we have looked at the criteria for assessing the quality of the selection evidence, we will summarize the entire contents.

screens.title: Read the model map using five criteria
screens.lead: Let's organize the standards established in this class by connecting them to the first question.

paragraphs: The first question was, by what criteria would the model begin to appear? Now there are five criteria. The grade indicates the role the model plays, the inference strength indicates the balance of speed, cost, and quality within the same model, the context and output limit indicate the amount that can be handled at once, multimodal support indicates the type of input that can be received, and the model ID and version indicate exactly which model was used.

Among these, limits and input format determine whether the task is possible, while class and inference strength determine which of the possible models is most appropriate. So, the general flow is to filter candidates based on input format and limit, select a grade based on difficulty and delay, and finally adjust the inference strength.

Choices should always be based on evidence. Write down at least two of the following: task difficulty, required delay, input length, and cost. If possible, experiment with the same inputs to find the lightest setting that satisfies your criteria. Even if a new model comes out, you can just put it on the same table.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: A good choice is not the biggest or newest model, but the lightest setup that meets the needs of the job.

checks.q: The quality of document classification work is sufficient, but response is slow and expensive. What are some options to try first?
options: Find the lightest setting for the same model that reduces inference strength and respects quality standards.
Switch to a larger model one level higher to ensure greater response quality.
Change model ID from alias to snapshot to speed up response
Reduce latency by switching to a model with a larger context window
checks.explain: You can balance speed, cost, and quality by adjusting effort without changing the model, and it is recommended to experiment with the same input to choose the lightest setting that satisfies the criteria.

wrong.1: Larger models are usually slower and more expensive, which adds to the problem.
wrong.2: The difference between aliases and snapshots is related to version pinning and does not increase speed.
wrong.3: Window size is a matter of how much it can hold, not a solution to latency.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match your next task with the rationale you will look for first in your model selection.
left: Work that must be reproduced later under the same conditions
right: Check whether images are supported in the input format row
Accuracy and limits first, starting from a higher grade or higher intensity
Latency and cost are important, so consider lightweight models
checks.explain: The key reasons are delay and cost for repetitive and bulk work, whether or not images support input, limit and accuracy for long documents, and ID and version history for reproduction.
checks.intro: Let’s check what we looked at earlier with one problem. There are no records or grading, so feel free to solve it.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

checks.q: I wrote down the basis for model selection. What is the most persuasive basis for judgment?
options: Because it is the largest model, it is the safest for any task.
It is best if the name has the latest version number attached to it.
Another team is already using the same model, so they follow suit.
Long input length and low required delay meet limits and response speed
checks.explain: A good rationale is to specify at least two of the following: task difficulty, required delay, input length, and cost. Size or newer name alone are not sufficient basis for judgment.

wrong.0: Being the biggest is a weak argument and may not be appropriate for tasks where delay and cost are critical.
wrong.1: The fact that a name is new does not demonstrate its relevance to the task.
wrong.2: The fact that someone else is writing is not connected to the needs of my work.

checks.intro: Please choose with the intention of organizing what you have learned. Results are not saved.

glossary.def: Within the same series, there are large, medium, and light levels with different performance, speed, and price.
Settings that control the amount of thought and output the model spends per request. Balance speed, cost, and quality without changing models.
This is an upper limit on the amount of input tokens that can be handled at one time and the output tokens that can be generated.
The ability to receive input such as images, audio, and PDF in addition to text.
A string that specifies the model in the API. There is a distinction between aliases and snapshots, and even IDs are recorded if reproduction is necessary.

misconceptions.myth: The largest model is always best.
misconceptions.fact: Larger models are usually slower and more expensive. For simple, high-volume tasks like classification, lightweight models are more appropriate in terms of latency and cost.

misconceptions.myth: Quality and speed can be controlled only by changing the model.
misconceptions.fact: The Claude documentation explains that adjusting effort is often a better tool than changing the model. The same model can also be balanced by inference strength.

misconceptions.myth: If the name is the same, the operation is also the same.
misconceptions.fact: Behavior may vary if the version changes. If you need to recreate the results, you should also record the model ID and version.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Models are divided into large, medium, and light grades, and each grade has a different role.
Inference strength is a setting that balances speed, cost, and quality without changing the model.
Context/output limits and multimodal support determine whether work is possible independently of level.
You must also record the model ID and version to recreate the same conditions.
Reasons for selection include at least two of the following: difficulty, delay, input length, and cost.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Pick a task that you frequently assign to AI and explain what level it would be at based on difficulty, delay, and input format.
